The ferry left the harbour at six, before the fog had lifted off the water. The captain had made the crossing more than four hundred times, and he steered the way other men drove to work, without thinking about the route. On the car deck the crew stacked crates of oranges and boxes of machine parts, roped them down, and checked the knots twice. A boy in a yellow jacket carried a clipboard from bow to stern, counting passengers as they came aboard. The engines coughed once and settled into a low steady hum that could be felt through the floor of the cabin, and the smell of diesel mixed with the salt air and the coffee from the little galley at the back.

In the lounge, a group of schoolchildren ate sandwiches from plastic boxes and argued about a video game. An old woman in a green coat read a newspaper folded into a narrow strip, her lips moving slightly. Two fishermen slept against the window, their caps pulled over their eyes. Outside, the water was grey and flat, and the far shore appeared and disappeared behind curtains of mist. The boy with the clipboard stopped at the top of the stairs, wrote something down, looked at his watch, and wrote something else.

At seven the captain came on the speaker. His voice was calm and a little bored. He said the crossing would take about twenty minutes longer than usual because of the visibility, that the cafe would stay open, and that passengers should keep their belongings with them. A few people looked up; most did not. The schoolchildren went on arguing, the old woman turned a page, and the fishermen did not move at all.

The mate came down to the lounge a few minutes later with a clipboard of his own. He stood by the door and counted the passengers again, quietly, moving his finger from row to row. Then he walked to the front and spoke to the boy in the yellow jacket, who nodded and went below. The engines changed note, a little deeper now, and the ship began to roll more than it had before. A paper cup slid across a table and fell on the floor, and someone laughed.

It was around half past seven, when the fog had thinned enough to show a line of white houses on the headland, that the captain announced the weekly drill. He explained that the crew would now walk the decks and check the safety equipment, that the lifeboat hatches would be opened and closed, and that nobody needed to move or worry. The words came through the speaker with the same calm he had used for the weather. The schoolchildren stopped talking for a moment, and the old woman folded her paper and held it in her lap.

Two members of the crew went along the deck with a torch and a notebook, stopping at each station. They lifted a cover, looked inside, wrote something down, and closed it again. At the stern they opened the hatch and let it fall back with a heavy sound that carried through the ship. The fishermen woke up, looked at one another, and went back to sleep. The boy in the yellow jacket came up the stairs and stood by the rail, watching the headland come closer.

By eight the sun had burned off the last of the mist, and the harbour wall was visible ahead, grey and long, with a few cars waiting on the quay. The engines slowed. The captain came on the speaker one more time to say they would be alongside in ten minutes, to remind drivers to return to the car deck, and to thank everyone for travelling. The passengers gathered their bags and coats, the old woman put her newspaper in her bag, and the schoolchildren pushed toward the stairs in a noisy crowd. The ferry turned, the hull touched the wall, and the ropes went out.
